strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates an important, under-modeled problem: heterogeneity in judge reliability in the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm and its consequences for biased rankings and invalid uncertainty quantification.

Clean and rigorous statistical formulation: a judge-aware BTL model with a discrimination-type reliability parameter, with formal identifiability results (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3) and asymptotic theory (consistency and asymptotic normality, Theorem 3.4) that support principled confidence intervals for score differences and rankings.

Simulation studies convincingly validate the theoretical claims: MSE decays at the predicted O(1/T) rate, and the judge-aware model achieves near-nominal coverage while the unweighted BTL model shows systematic and worsening under-coverage as T grows, illustrating the 'confidently wrong' phenomenon motivating the paper.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across multiple real datasets (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, and a new in-house 45-model dataset), with face-validity checks (e.g., correct GPT-4/Claude ordering, Vicuna-13B > Vicuna-7B, agreement with published MT-Bench rankings) and quantitative comparison to human-derived Chatbot Arena rankings (Spearman correlation improvement).

Practical, implementable estimation procedure (aggregated likelihood, Adam-based optimization with normalization constraints) with reported efficiency gains (narrower CIs, higher data efficiency) over the unweighted baseline.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core idea (judge/annotator-specific discrimination parameters analogous to 2PL IRT models) closely parallels Otani et al. (2016) and existing BTL asymptotic theory (e.g., Gao et al. 2023; Fan et al. 2024b), and the paper does not clearly delineate what is technically new beyond extending this design to a fully randomized, reference-free judge panel.

The efficiency evaluation in Section 5.3 is partly circular: the 'ground truth' used to assess subsampling efficiency is the full-data fit of the same (weighted or unweighted) model, not an independent gold standard, so the reported efficiency gains partly reflect self-consistency of each method with itself rather than closeness to true model quality.

No empirical comparison to existing LLM-ranking baselines discussed in related work (REM, GTR/FTR, Product-of-Experts), despite these being explicitly positioned as competitors; only the unweighted BTL model is used as a baseline throughout.

The i.i.d. uniform random design assumption underlying the asymptotic theory is unlikely to hold for the real datasets (comparisons are typically unbalanced across pairs/judges), and the paper does not discuss or empirically assess robustness of the inferential guarantees to this mismatch.
Tie handling (encoding ties as y=0.5) is ad hoc and not derived from the probabilistic model, potentially biasing the likelihood in datasets with many ties (mentioned as present in real datasets).

Judge reliability is assumed static across all comparisons/tasks; the exclusion of a judge with γ̂≈0 due to numerical instability suggests potential fragility of the estimator in edge cases that is not deeply investigated.

Human-preference validation is somewhat limited: a single Spearman correlation comparison on Chatbot Arena (0.9955 vs 0.9699) without confidence intervals, significance testing, or broader replication across datasets to substantiate the claimed improvement in alignment with human preference.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical treatment: the paper proves identifiability (up to a natural scale/location normalization), consistency, and asymptotic normality of the MLE for the judge-aware BTL model, with detailed, largely self-contained proofs in the appendix (Fisher information invertibility via a weighted Gram-matrix argument, uniform LLN arguments, Delta method transfer from the free parameterization back to (s, gamma)).

Comprehensive empirical validation spanning simulations (confirming O(1/T) convergence and calibrated coverage vs. under-coverage of the unweighted BTL baseline) and four real-world benchmarks (MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, UltraFeedback, and a newly collected 45-model/18-judge dataset), with consistent qualitative conclusions across all of them.

The Chatbot Arena case study is a compelling demonstration: the weighted model corrects an intuitively wrong unweighted ranking (GPT-4 dropping to 3rd) and achieves higher Spearman correlation with human-preference-based BTL rankings (0.9955 vs 0.9699).

Multiple robustness checks are included (tie-handling ablation, sparse/connected comparison-graph subsampling, a length-covariate extension of the judge discrimination parameter), which strengthens confidence that the core findings are not artifacts of specific design choices.

The paper provides a practical, well-documented optimization algorithm (projected Adam with explicit gradient formulas) and reports data efficiency gains (narrower CIs, higher correlation to reference scores) that are plausible and consistent with the theory.
Clear discussion of limitations (global scalar discrimination parameter, conditional independence assumption, sparse/imbalanced designs) rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution—multiplying a judge-specific scalar discrimination parameter into a BTL log-odds, akin to a 2-parameter IRT model—is conceptually close to prior IRT-based pairwise aggregation (Otani et al., 2016); the delta (reference-free, fully randomized design, asymptotic theory) is real but incremental rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea.

No direct empirical comparison against the explicitly discussed competing methods REM and GTR/FTR, despite these being positioned as the main prior art for LLM ranking without ground truth; only the unweighted BTL baseline is compared throughout, which is the easiest baseline to beat and does not establish superiority over existing heuristic weighting schemes.

The validation that gamma correctly identifies 'high-quality' vs 'low-quality' judges (Section 5.4) relies on informal, subjective a priori labeling by the authors rather than an independent, rigorous ground-truth measure of judge quality (e.g., correlation with large-scale human annotations per judge), weakening the causal claim that gamma captures 'true' reliability rather than some other artifact (e.g., verbosity, confidence calibration, or self-similarity to the aggregated ranking it is fit against).

The model assumes conditionally independent judge errors and a single global (or, in the appendix extension, length-covariate) discrimination parameter per judge; this ignores well-documented judge-specific biases in LLM-as-judge settings (self-preference/self-enhancement bias, position bias, verbosity bias), which are arguably more consequential confounds than generic 'noise' and are not modeled or empirically probed despite being highly relevant to the framework's real-world reliability.

The magnitude of the reported efficiency gains (e.g., 5.4%–13.5% CI-width reduction) is fairly modest, and it is unclear whether this translates into materially different practical leaderboard decisions beyond the illustrative GPT-4 ranking anomaly.

The central motivating claim that 'more data can make evaluation more confidently wrong' is demonstrated only under a simulation explicitly constructed so the unweighted model is misspecified relative to the true data-generating process—an expected consequence of model misspecification rather than a surprising empirical finding about real judge panels.
